final_proof:
We use the following standard consequence of Ingham's prime-gap theorem: there are constants C > 0 and X_0 such that, for every real x >= X_0, some prime q satisfies

    x < q < x + C x^(5/8).

We first derive the precise consequence that we need. Choose an integer M so large that M^3 >= X_0 and C m^(15/8) < 2m^2 for every integer m >= M; this is possible because 15/8 < 2. Applying Ingham's theorem with x = m^3 shows that, for every integer m >= M, there is a prime q for which

    m^3 < q < m^3 + C m^(15/8) < m^3 + 2m^2.

In particular,

    m^3 < q  and  q + 1 < m^3 + 2m^2 + 1 < (m+1)^3.    (1)

Choose a prime p_1 >= M (primes are unbounded), and construct primes p_2, p_3, ... recursively. Once p_n has been chosen, apply (1) with m = p_n and choose a prime p_(n+1) such that

    p_n^3 < p_(n+1)  and  p_(n+1) + 1 < (p_n+1)^3.    (2)

This recursion can continue indefinitely: (2) implies p_(n+1) > p_n, so every p_n is at least M and the preceding consequence of Ingham's theorem remains applicable.

For n >= 1 define

    a_n = p_n^(1/3^n),       b_n = (p_n+1)^(1/3^n).

Both sides in (2) are positive. Taking 3^(n+1)-st roots there gives

    a_n < a_(n+1)  and  b_(n+1) < b_n.    (3)

Thus (a_n) is increasing. It is bounded above by b_1, since a_n < b_n <= b_1, so by completeness of the real numbers it has a limit; put

    A = lim_(n to infinity) a_n.

For every fixed n, clearly A >= a_n. Moreover, all the a_k are at most b_(n+1) once k <= n+1 by monotonicity of (a_k), and once k >= n+1 because a_k < b_k <= b_(n+1). Hence A <= b_(n+1). By (3), b_(n+1) < b_n, and consequently

    a_n <= A < b_n.

Raising this inequality to the positive integer power 3^n yields

    p_n <= A^(3^n) < p_n+1.

Therefore floor(A^(3^n)) = p_n, which is prime, for every n in N_{>0}. This proves the claim.
